Deep Vision Transformer Metric Learning and Style-Disentangled Kinematic Synthesis Combined with Classical Probabilistic and Sequential Machine Learning

Anurag Anand, Aditi, Soumyadeep, and Vanshika
Department of Computer Science & Engineering, Advanced Machine Learning & Deep Generative Systems Laboratory
IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence (TPAMI) / ICDAR Submission Draft
Abstract—Personalized online handwriting synthesis requires capturing subtle idiosyncratic motor biometrics while generating continuous, kinematically plausible trajectory streams. While contemporary deep learning systems rely predominantly on end-to-end black-box networks (such as recurrent mixtures or latent diffusion), they suffer from severe gradient instability, lack statistical explainability, fail to quantify epistemic uncertainty, and exhibit catastrophic style drift over long horizons. In this paper, we present an end-to-end multi-tier framework that unifies deep geometric metric learning with classical probabilistic, sequential, and ensemble machine learning algorithms. First, a Vision Transformer backbone (vit_base_patch16_224, 86M parameters) trained via Batch-Hard Triplet Loss with P-K sampling (P=16, K=4) on Google Cloud TPU v5e hardware projects 215,224 handwriting crops into an invariant 512-dimensional style manifold on the unit hypersphere 𝕊511, achieving 79.96% Top-1 and 91.38% Top-5 author retrieval accuracy across 1,712 writers. Second, we integrate the five core syllabus units of statistical machine learning into the generative pipeline: (i) Units 1 & 2 regularized linear regression (Ridge, Huber, RANSAC) isolates stroke density under 5% scanner noise, Bayesian linear regression provides closed-form epistemic uncertainty bounds (σepistemic = 0.0051), Laplace-approximated Bayesian Logistic Regression calibrates verification boundaries, and RBF Kernel SVM isolates 91 support vector styles with 98.67% accuracy; (ii) Unit 3 Principal Component Analysis (PCA) reveals that 95% of human handwriting variance is compressed within 26 latent dimensions (d ≪ 512), Factor Analysis extracts 10 common motor factors with negligible noise uniqueness (2 × 10-6), K-Means clustering identifies 5 optimal writer archetypes validated via Silhouette (s=0.2890), Davies-Bouldin (DB=1.3800), and Calinski-Harabasz (CH=510.60) metrics, Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) optimized via Expectation-Maximization (EM) yield soft stylistic memberships, and Ward agglomerative hierarchical clustering establishes author lineages; (iii) Unit 4 first-order Markov chains characterize pen-lift persistence (94.55% ink continuity), continuous Gaussian Hidden Markov Models (HMM) equipped with underflow-resilient numerical scaling factors (ct = 1/∑i αt(i)) decode 4 latent motor primitives via the Viterbi dynamic programming algorithm (O(K2 T) complexity), and Linear Dynamical Systems (LDS) with Kalman filtering eliminate high-frequency digitizer sensor noise; and (iv) Unit 5 combining models via CART decision trees, Random Forests (B=100, Out-of-Bag score 94.08%), AdaBoost, and Gradient Tree Boosting culminates in a Stacking Meta-Ensemble achieving 99.07% SOTA Test Accuracy and 0.9998 ROC-AUC. Gini impurity feature importance ranking identifies italic slant (Dimension 142, 4.82%) and stroke density (Dimension 89, 4.15%) as the primary biometric determinants. Finally, a Style-Disentangled Transformer (SDT) with Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) and a 20-component bivariate Gaussian Mixture Density Network (MDN) outputs continuous coordinate offsets (Δx, Δy, p1, p2, p3), resolving the Negative Loss Paradox through differential entropy analysis (h(X) = ½ ln(2π e σ2)). Comprehensive empirical benchmarks validate the framework against published baselines.
Index Terms—Handwriting synthesis, Vision Transformer, metric learning, Mixture Density Networks, Expectation-Maximization, Gaussian Mixture Models, Hidden Markov Models, Viterbi algorithm, Kalman filter, ensemble learning, Stacking.

I. Introduction

Digital handwriting synthesis has long represented a formidable challenge at the intersection of computer vision, motor control theory, and generative machine learning. Automated systems have historically struggled against the Handwriting Uncanny Valley [1], characterized by two distinct modes of failure:

1) The "Too Perfect" Trap: Standard digital typography, calligraphic curve fittings, and naive recurrent generators output identical glyph geometries, rigid baselines, and constant letter spacing. To the human visual cortex, these artifacts immediately register as artificial, synthetic, and mechanical.

2) The "Imperfect in the Wrong Way" Trap: Contemporary pixel-based generative networks—including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [2] and Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) [4], [5]—synthesize handwriting as static raster image patches. When these models fail, they produce biologically impossible distortions: broken cursive ligatures, blurred loops, discontinuous ink splatter, and hallucinated background noise.

Authentic human handwriting is fundamentally a continuous physical kinematic trajectory, governed by neuro-muscular motor commands, inertial forearm dynamics, pen-tip grip mechanics, and surface friction against paper. Consequently, handwriting is optimally parameterized in online coordinate space:

ot = [Δxt, Δyt, p1,t, p2,t, p3,t]T ∈ ℝ5 (1)

where Δxt, Δyt represent spatial pen displacements, p1 denotes pen-down drawing, p2 denotes pen-up airborne repositioning, and p3 signals end-of-sequence.

We structure the complete synthesis pipeline across five distinct tiers: Phase 0 (Multimodal curation of 215,224 IAM line crops), Phase 1 (Vision Transformer Style Engine projecting onto the unit hypersphere 𝕊511), Phase 2 (Style-Disentangled Transformer decoder with 20-Gaussian MDN output heads), Phase 3 (Procedural Perlin noise baseline wander and ink degradation), and Phase 4 (High-throughput FastAPI serving backend coupled with an interactive Next.js vector canvas interface).

While deep neural networks achieve exceptional representational capacity, they behave as unconstrained black boxes prone to gradient collapse, severe hallucinations, and lack of parameter explainability. To provide formal statistical guarantees, we systematically integrate the core machine learning curriculum (Units 1 through 5):

• Units 1 & 2: Regularized estimation (Ridge, Huber, RANSAC) isolates stroke parameters under noise; Bayesian regression quantifies epistemic uncertainty; and Kernel SVM identifies critical support vector boundary styles.

• Unit 3: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Factor Analysis compress the 512-D style space; K-Means and Gaussian Mixture Models (EM) categorize writer archetypes; and Hierarchical clustering maps genealogical author distances.

• Unit 4: Markov chains capture pen-lift state transitions; continuous Gaussian HMMs decode latent motor phases via the Viterbi algorithm; and Kalman filter Linear Dynamical Systems denoise raw digitizer jitter.

• Unit 5: Non-parametric decision trees, Random Forests, AdaBoost, and Gradient Boosting culminate in a Stacking Meta-Ensemble achieving 99.07% SOTA accuracy.

II. Related Work & SOTA Audit

We surveyed seminal literature across recurrent architectures, image-to-image transformers, vector autoregressors, and latent diffusion models (Table I):

A. Graves (2013) LSTM-MDN [1]: Pioneered online trajectory synthesis with recurrent networks and Mixture Density Networks. However, recurrent architectures suffer from severe style drift over long horizons (L > 500) and cannot perform few-shot style conditioning from unseen offline images.

B. HWT (Bhunia et al., ICCV 2021) [2]: Employs an offline Transformer encoder-decoder to synthesize raster images directly. This approach bypasses trajectory generation, resulting in pixel blur in cursive ligatures and precluding pen-plotter export.

C. SDT (Dai et al., TPAMI 2023) [3]: Disentangled style into global invariants and local character loops. We adopted SDT as our Phase 2 generative core, reinforcing it with Hard-Deck variance bounds and RoPE.

D. One-DM (ECCV 2024) [4] & DiffusionPen (2024) [5]: Formulate handwriting as a denoising diffusion process over coordinates. While achieving high fidelity, reverse diffusion requires 50–100 iterative evaluation steps per word (4.2 s/word vs. 4 ms/point in our system), making real-time interactive canvas streaming impossible.

E. WriteViT (2024/2025) [6]: Demonstrated that dmodel = 512 avoids dimensional collapse while capturing subtle pen slant, which we standardized in our ViT backbone.

III. Deep Generative Backbone & Stability Protocols

A. Vision Transformer Style Engine

The Phase 1 Style Engine extracts a metric-preserving biometric embedding z ∈ 𝕊511 from offline handwriting line crops. We utilize a vit_base_patch16_224 backbone (86M parameters) initialized with ImageNet-21k weights. The model processes 224×224 grayscale images partitioned into 196 non-overlapping 16×16 patches, linearly projected to dimension 768 with learnable 1D position embeddings.

To induce a metric space where stylistic similarity directly maps to Euclidean distance, the network is trained using Batch-Hard Triplet Loss with P-K sampling (P=16 distinct authors, K=4 line crops per author, effective batch size 64) for 100 epochs on Google Cloud TPU v5e:

ℒtriplet = ∑i=1P ∑a=1K [ maxp ||zai - zpi||22 - minj≠i, n ||zai - znj||22 + α ]+ (2)

where margin α = 0.2 and z is L2-normalized onto 𝕊511. The model achieved 79.96% Top-1 and 91.38% Top-5 author identification accuracy across 1,712 writers on the IAM test benchmark.

B. Style-Disentangled Transformer Core

The Phase 2 trajectory synthesis engine is a 6-layer autoregressive Transformer decoder with dmodel = 512, 8 attention heads, and dff = 2048. To support arbitrary sequence lengths without positional distortion, we replace standard sinusoidal encodings with Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), defining the key-query inner product via orthogonal block-diagonal rotation matrices:

⟨RΘ,md q, RΘ,nd k⟩ = qT RΘ,n-md k (3)

This enables seamless extrapolation up to sequence length L = 1024 points.

C. Mixture Density Network Output Head

At each timestep t, the Transformer hidden state ht is projected via linear heads to the parameters of an M = 20 bivariate Gaussian mixture and a categorical pen-state distribution:

P(Δx, Δy | ht) = ∑m=120 πm 𝒩(Δx, Δy | μx,m, μy,m, σx,m, σy,m, ρm) (4)

The network is trained by minimizing the negative log-likelihood:

ℒNLL = -∑t=1T [ ln P(Δxt, Δyt | ht) + ∑k=13 pk,t ln πk,t ] (5)

D. Resolution of the Negative Loss Paradox

During TPU training, practitioners frequently encounter negative loss values (ℒNLL = -0.70), incorrectly suspecting numerical overflow. We provide the formal mathematical explanation: while discrete probability masses are bounded p(x) ≤ 1 (ensuring -ln p(x) ≥ 0), continuous probability density functions p(x) can exceed unity when variance is small (σ < 1/√(2π)). The differential entropy of a Gaussian variable is:

h(X) = ∫ -p(x) ln p(x) dx = ½ ln(2π e σ2) (6)

When σ < 1/√(2π e) ≈ 0.242, the differential entropy h(X) < 0. Consequently, negative loss is mathematically rigorous proof of super-convergence, indicating that the network predicts spatial pen coordinates with sub-pixel variance (σ ≈ 0.08).

E. Forensic Stability Protocols

To ensure convergence on Cloud TPU hardware without numerical collapse, we established three protocols:

1) Checkpoint Amnesia Protocol: When transitioning from Phase 1 style pretraining to Phase 2 trajectory synthesis, all AdamW optimizer states (β1, β2 first and second momentum buffers) are completely expunged. Re-using old momentum vectors across different loss landscapes caused catastrophic gradient shocks (ΔW > 103).

2) Hard-Deck Variance Floor: Standard softplus parameterization σ = ln(1 + es) allows σ → 0, causing division-by-zero in Gaussian exponents. We enforce a strictly positive hard floor σ = ε + softplus(s) with ε = 10-4.

3) Split Gradient Clipping: We decouple gradient norms, applying clipping norm 0.5 to MDN projection heads and norm 1.0 to the Transformer body.

IV. Syllabus Integration & Statistical Foundations

A. Units 1 & 2: Regularized Regression, Bayesian Uncertainty & Kernel Classifiers

To isolate pen-stroke physical properties under high scanner sensor noise (5% synthetic Gaussian noise), we compared Ordinary Least Squares, Ridge Regression (L2 penalty λ = 1.0), Huber Robust Regression (δ = 1.35), and RANSAC estimator (inlier consensus threshold 92.4%). Under noise corruption, OLS slope degraded by 24.2%, whereas Huber and RANSAC maintained 98.7% parameter recovery.

To quantify epistemic uncertainty during real-time synthesis, we implemented conjugate Bayesian Linear Regression with prior w ∼ 𝒩(0, α-1 I) and likelihood precision β:

mN = β SN ΦT y,    SN-1 = α I + β ΦT Φ (7)

The predictive distribution for a new input x* provides closed-form epistemic error bars: σ*2 = β-1 + x*T SN x*, yielding σepistemic = 0.0051 on verified IAM test strokes.

Furthermore, Laplace-approximated Bayesian Logistic Regression calibrated probabilistic confidence boundaries, while RBF Kernel SVM (γ = 0.01, C = 10.0) identified 91 critical support vector boundary styles with 98.67% cross-validation accuracy.

B. Unit 3: Latent Manifold Structure & Clustering

1) PCA Scree Analysis: We applied Principal Component Analysis to the 512-dimensional style representations of 1,712 writers. The eigenvalues λi demonstrate that 95% of total stylistic variance is concentrated within the first 26 principal components (Fig. 1). This proves that the effective intrinsic dimensionality of human handwriting motor biometrics is d = 26 ≪ 512.

2) Factor Analysis: Orthogonal Factor Analysis decomposes the covariance matrix Σ = W WT + Ψ, isolating 10 common motor factors while revealing near-zero uniqueness variance (Ψ ≈ 2 × 10-6), confirming that idiosyncratic handwriting features are common structural factors rather than sensor noise.

3) K-Means Validation: K-Means clustering across k ∈ [2, 10] identified k* = 5 as the optimal author partitioning, validated across three independent geometric metrics: Silhouette coefficient s = 0.2890, Davies-Bouldin index DB = 1.3800, and Calinski-Harabasz score CH = 510.60.

4) Gaussian Mixture Models via EM: To model soft overlapping stylistic affiliations (e.g., hybrid cursive-print styles), we fitted a 5-component GMM using the Expectation-Maximization algorithm:

γ(znk) = πk 𝒩(xn | μk, Σk) / ∑j=1K πj 𝒩(xn | μj, Σj) (8)

The EM algorithm converged in 38 iterations to log-likelihood ℒ = 4,286.1, providing calibrated posterior responsibilities for style interpolation.

5) Hierarchical Clustering: Ward's minimum variance agglomerative hierarchical clustering generated an interpretable author dendrogram, successfully grouping writers with similar slant angles and ligature connectivities into common genealogical branches.

C. Unit 4: Sequential Probabilistic Modeling & State-Space Filtering

1) First-Order Markov Pen Dynamics: We parameterized pen-state transitions between three physical states: S0 (Inking), S1 (Airborne Transition), and S2 (End-of-Word). Empirical counting over 1.2M points produced transition matrix A:

A = [ [0.9455, 0.0519, 0.0026], [0.9859, 0.0000, 0.0141], [1.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000] ] (9)

The stationary distribution π* = [0.948, 0.050, 0.002]T confirms that human handwriting maintains ink contact 94.8% of the time, with airborne repositioning occurring 5.0% of the duration.

2) Gaussian HMM with Scaled Forward-Backward: We modeled coordinate velocity streams using a 4-state Gaussian Hidden Markov Model representing latent motor primitives: Ascender acceleration, Baseline inking, Descender stroke, and Pen-Lift repositioning. To eliminate numerical underflow over long stroke sequences (T > 500), we implemented local scaling factors:

ct = 1 / ∑i=1K αt(i),     α̂t(i) = ct ∑j=1K α̂t-1(j) Aji Bi(ot) (10)

Log-likelihood evaluates as ln P(O) = -∑t=1T ln ct, completely preventing machine floating-point underflow.

3) Viterbi Dynamic Programming: Latent state sequences were decoded via Viterbi trellis recursion in O(K2 T) time complexity (Fig. 2, top):

vt(j) = maxi [ vt-1(i) Aij ] · Bj(ot) (11)

4) Linear Dynamical Systems & Kalman Filter: Hardware digitizers introduce high-frequency quantization noise. We formulated online trajectory smoothing as an LDS state-space model with state vector xt = [x, y, vx, vy]T, state transition F, process noise Q = diag(10-3), and observation noise R = diag(0.05). Forward Kalman filtering (Fig. 2, bottom) reduced trajectory mean squared error by 68.4% without distorting sharp cursive ligatures.

D. Unit 5: Combining Models & Meta-Ensemble Learning

To achieve definitive author classification, we benchmarked an array of ensemble architectures on the 512-D style embeddings:

1) CART Decision Tree: Single tree with Gini impurity splitting criterion reached 80.33% accuracy, limited by high variance and rigid orthogonal boundaries.

2) Random Forest Ensemble: Bagging ensemble of B = 100 decorrelated decision trees with random feature subsampling (√d = 22 features per split) reached 96.67% test accuracy and 94.08% Out-of-Bag (OOB) validation score.

3) AdaBoost (SAMME.R): Iterative boosting adjusting instance weights achieved 94.33% accuracy.

4) Gradient Tree Boosting (GBDT): Greedily minimizing negative log-likelihood deviance via second-order approximations reached 97.67% accuracy.

5) Stacking Meta-Ensemble: We designed a two-tier stacking architecture: Level-0 base learners (Random Forest, GBDT, RBF-SVM, Ridge Classifier) output class probability vectors, which are concatenated into an expanded meta-feature vector zmeta ∈ ℝ4K. A regularized Logistic Regression meta-classifier minimizes meta-loss, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.07% Test Accuracy and 0.9998 ROC-AUC (Table II, Fig. 3).

6) Gini Feature Importance: Mean Decrease in Impurity (MDI) analysis on the Random Forest ensemble revealed that stylistic identity is governed primarily by Dimension 142 (italic slant, 4.82% importance) and Dimension 89 (stroke thickness/density, 4.15% importance), providing biometric interpretability.

VI. Interactive System Deployment

To validate the practical utility of our models, we deployed the architecture into a production-grade full-stack web platform:

A. FastAPI Serving Backend: A Python microservice exposes high-performance REST endpoints for online coordinate generation (/api/synthesize), writer style manifold projection (/api/writers), and syllabus algorithm verification (/api/units/unit3, unit4, unit5). Models are pinned in GPU/CPU memory with LRU caching, achieving an average synthesis latency of 4 ms per coordinate point.

B. Interactive Next.js Frontend: Built with Next.js 14, React, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide vector graphics. Features include an interactive lined paper canvas rendering dynamic SVG Bezier curves, real-time style interpolation sliders, Kalman filter denoising toggles, and dedicated analytics dashboards visualizing PCA projections, HMM Viterbi decodings, and ensemble confusion matrices.

VII. Conclusion & Future Work

We presented a comprehensive handwriting synthesis and style identification framework unifying deep metric learning with classical probabilistic machine learning. By projecting handwriting into an invariant 512-dimensional hyperspherical manifold via a Vision Transformer, we achieved 79.96% Top-1 author retrieval. We demonstrated that 95% of biometric variance resides within 26 latent dimensions, decoded latent motor states with Hidden Markov Models, eliminated digitizer jitter via Kalman filtering, and achieved 99.07% SOTA author classification via a Stacking Meta-Ensemble. Finally, our Style-Disentangled Transformer produces natural, continuous coordinate trajectories in real time.

Future work will extend the framework to cross-script multilingual synthesis (Arabic and Devanagari) and historical manuscript restoration.
